newsitem.title: GERMANY: German govt report sees '97 deficit 2.9 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: German govt report sees '97 deficit 2.9 pct of GDP.

text.p: Germany's annual government economic report, to be published on Tuesday, forecasts a public sector budget deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product, according to a copy obtained by Reuters on Monday.

The forecast is an upward revision from the 2.5 percent deficit predicted by Finance Minister Theo Waigel when the budget was passed late last year. Germany wants the deficit to be below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent this year in order to qualify for European monetary union in 1999.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet is due on Tuesday to review the report, which predicts growth of 2.5 percent -- in line with budget assumptions -- but expects the unemployment rate to jump to 11 percent from 10.3 percent in 1996.

The higher deficit forecast leaves Waigel with very little room for manoeuvre to meet Germany's goal of hitting the strict Maastricht deficit target -- a goal which both Bonn and the Bundesbank have avowed.

Juergen Stark, Waigel's number two in the Finance Ministry, told Monday's Handelsblatt newspaper he was convinced Germany would not have to exploit the leeway written into the treaty to qualify for monetary union.
"I am convinced that Germany will meet the Maastricht criteria. Everyone must work towards that!" Stark was quoted by Handelsblatt as saying.
"The euro starting group must guarantee that the common European currency will be stable," he added.
